text: One of the most important lessons that I had to learn in my life
is that when it comes to our growth and development,
there is no substitute for a tough piece of feedback
from someone who cares about us.
And when we can make it safe enough for the people in our lives
to tell us those hard things,
it not only benefits us,
it can spark transformation in our workplaces
and in our families.
And I learned this lesson the way that I learned most things,
which is the hard way,
and it was when I got a tough piece of feedback
from my best friend at work, Christy.
So I met Christy years ago
when I left the only organization I had ever worked for
to start over at a new company,
and I was freaking out.
And Christy was this incredibly kind and welcoming person
who just really went out of her way to help me be successful.
And we became fast friends.
And then one day we got into an argument.
Not uncommon for us --
we’re both pretty stubborn and opinionated people --
and we resolved it, and I thought everything was fine.
She had a very different reaction,
and the next day she came in
and she gave me this feedback, and I'll never forget it.
She said,
"It just seemed like while we were arguing
that you needed me to feel stupid.”
And if you've ever had somebody make you feel that way,
you know it’s awful.
So here's my best friend at work,
somebody that I care about,
she's told me that I've hurt her,
and so of course, my immediate reaction
is I get very defensive.
So I remember I was like,
running through all of this in my head, right?
Like, "How could you say that?
That's completely unfair.
I would never think that about you."
And then I was just listing off all the reasons that she was wrong.
(Laughter)
Now, thankfully,
I didn't say any of that out loud.
And --
(Laughter)
All I could think to say in the moment was,
"Thank you for telling me."
And I meant it because she could have done so many other things, right?
She could have gossiped about me behind my back,
she could have gone to our boss and complained about me,
she could have done what I probably would have done,
which is just silently resent me and not said anything.
(Laughter)
But she had the courage to come and talk to me.
And the truth is, I've gotten this feedback before.
And the feedback is that when I'm not at my best,
I come across as arrogant,
condescending, self-righteous and a know-it-all --
which is a really nice combination
and a great way to make friends, if you're interested.
(Laughter)
It's the thing in my life I am most embarrassed about
and oftentimes ashamed of.
And so I'm telling this to Christy and I say,
“I know I do this, and I’m sorry.
I don't want to,
but I can't hear myself when I'm doing it.
Can you help me?"
And she says, "Sure, I'll just tell you when you're doing it."
Not like that, I meant, “Do you have a book I could read or like,
I don't know, like a training or something like that
that I could take, you know, to fix this?”
And she said, "Well, how about this?
I'll just say 'You're doing your thing.'"
Worth a shot.
So anytime we'd be talking and I would start a sentence with,
"Well, actually," or something like that,
she would just, "Hey, Chris, you're doing your thing."
And it was so helpful.
I needed the feedback.
I could start to hear it
and so I could start to improve on it.
[A] little embarrassed to find out how often I do it,
but I did start to get better,
and I noticed the transformation of my relationships almost immediately.
My wife would later tell me that this whole process,
it made it easier for her to talk to me,
and that allowed us to have conversations
that we hadn't been able to have up until that point.
So I'm growing,
my relationships are transforming.
And then it started to inspire other people to do the same thing.
And it started with Christy.
She came to me one day,
"What's my thing?"
(Laughter)
And I kind of think we all have a thing, right?
Like something that we do that we're not at our best,
gets in our way.
And so Christy's thing,
and I have her permission to share this,
is -- just be clear --
is that when she gets upset and she's not at her best,
she can go from zero to 100 [in] about two seconds,
and she'll say something she regrets.
OK, so she says,
“Yeah, that’s it.
And you're going to tell me when I'm doing it."
No, no.
(Laughter)
Absolutely not.
Are you serious?
"I've been doing it for you,
you have to do it for me.”
Which is fair.
So first time I had to tell her
I'm terrified.
Remember, she's upset.
She's up here and I'm like,
"Hey, buddy ..."
(Laughter)
"I think you might be doing your thing."
And she instantly cools off and she looks at me and she says,
"Oh my gosh, you're right.
Thank you."
And then she started to improve.
And then I felt safer to keep giving her that feedback.
And both of us are like, we might be on to something here.
Then there’s a restructure in our department,
I become Christy's supervisor.
And one of the first things she says to me is,
"I'm just bummed I can't do that feedback thing with you anymore."
"Why?"
"You're my boss, I can't talk to you like that."
"No, I need you to talk to me like that."
And this is key because it's not just our own defensiveness
that gets in the way of people giving us the feedback.
There's these other barriers, like titles and roles,
that can make it feel scary to talk to us.
I imagine you're probably not going to walk into your CEO's office
or something like that,
"I have some thoughts on your performance I'd like to share with you."
Like, you're probably not going to do that.
I did have to do that once.
I had to give my CEO critical feedback,
and she gave me a hug.
And for just a second, I thought it was like one of those mafia-style hugs.
Like, "That was the biggest mistake you ever made,"
or something like that.
(Laughter)
But it was genuine
and it made me so proud to work for her.
So I'm telling this to Christy,
"You've got to keep giving me the feedback."
And that has not been a problem.
(Laughter)
But then it started to inspire other people to do the same thing.
So I've got this new team and they all come to me,
"We want to know what our thing is."
I've got managers in other areas,
"How do we make this happen on our teams?"
But where this really broke open for me
was one day when I was talking to my sister,
and I was telling her this story
and how I'm like, "Hey, somebody at work said
I can come across as arrogant and condescending.
Can you believe that?"
(Laughter)
And she paused
And she said, "Yeah."
And I was completely blindsided,
which doesn't make any sense, of course,
because she would have been one of the first people
to have to deal with this.
And it turns out it had bothered her for a long time.
But she hadn't talked to me about it.
And she told me
"There were times in my life that I really needed you,
but I didn't call
because I just didn't want to hear that tone."
And that was so painful to hear.
And it was the breakthrough moment in our relationship.
Because now when she has a problem with me, she can just tell me.
And that has meant everything to us.
And after that, I was like, I've got to get feedback from everyone.
So I do this with my boss, with my teammates,
I do this with my wife and son.
My son will say to me, "Dad, can I give you some feedback?"
I love it, I love it.
Usually, yeah.
(Laughter)
I don't always agree with it,
but I'm such a better dad because of it.
And more important than that
is that it means everything to me
that he feels safe enough to say that to me.
And I've also had the opportunity
to help hundreds of other people create similar experiences
in their own relationships.
Most of us, we want to have these important
and difficult conversations,
but we put too much pressure on the Christies of the world
to show up again and again
with the courage to say the hard thing.
And that's a mistake.
There's too many barriers to that happening consistently.
As feedback receivers,
we have to make it safer,
and we have to lower the amount of courage
that it requires to have that conversation.
Now, thankfully, this is a skill
that we can learn and that we can practice.
And if you want to, you can use an approach that I use
called receiving feedback with tact.
So if you want to try this,
pick someone in your life that you want some more feedback from,
someone who cares about you,
but they'll be honest with you if you make it a little bit safer.
Then don't wait for them to give you feedback,
go out and ask for it.
Just don't make the mistake that I made early on,
I was working with this group of managers and I said,
"Go out and get some feedback from some of your employees."
And they're like, "OK, how am I doing as your manager?"
And everyone was like, "Great!"
(Laughter)
"Why?"
(Laughter)
It's too scary, right?
We need to narrow that question.
So I might say,
"I want to get better at running our staff meetings.
What's one piece of advice you have for me on how I could improve?"
And then here's the key.
It's how you respond.
That's going to be the difference between you learning something
and building trust with this person,
or the opposite.
So when they give you the feedback that you asked for,
you can respond with tact.
So that stands for thankfulness,
acknowledgment,
commitment
and then we'll end where we began, a second thankfulness.
We'll take a brief look at each one.
So that first thankfulness,
you're trying to calm down that initial fight-or-flight response
that you might both be experiencing.
So I might say "That wasn't easy to hear,
but I'm really glad you were willing to say it."
With acknowledgment,
you want to make the other person feel seen and heard first,
because that's your entryway into an authentic dialogue.
They're expecting you to defend yourself,
and all that's going to do is it's just going to shut them down
or gear them up for a fight.
You don't have to agree.
Just acknowledge what they said,
acknowledge the feelings underneath what they said,
and then you can have a real conversation.
And that will eventually lead you to some kind of a commitment.
If you agree with the feedback,
it could be the behavior change you're going to make.
If you don't agree or you're not sure,
it could be to gather a few more perspectives and circle back.
It could be that you need a little bit of time and space to process,
but you're going to get back to them at a specific date and time.
Just be clear what's next and follow through.
And the second thankfulness is my favorite part
because it's so easy to do and it's very powerful.
What you're trying to do here is reinforce and reward the behavior
so that they keep doing it.
Most of us don't do things that are painful or unpleasant,
like giving feedback,
unless there's some sort of a benefit for doing it.
So when the conversation's over, send them a quick text.
"Thank you."
Or do what one of my colleagues did when I gave him tough feedback,
he wrote me a handwritten thank-you card.
Just do something that makes it feel like it was worth the risk to tell you.
So it's thankfulness, acknowledgment, commitment,
and then a second thankfulness.
Do this consistently
and you're going to be amazed at what you learn
and the ways that it starts to benefit your relationships.
There is likely someone in your life who cares about you
and has something to tell you that you might not want to hear,
but it could change your life if you did.
If you want the benefits of that feedback,
ask for it and then respond with tact.
I have seen it do wonders for so many people, including me.
As I was preparing for today,
I shared a draft with my sister and this is what she told me.
She said,
"Chris, you've completely flipped the way that you talk to me,
and I can't even remember what you used to sound like.
I can be completely myself around you, even though we're so different."
So go out and get a tough piece of feedback
from someone who cares about you
and let it change your life.
Thank you.
(Cheers and applause)
